The Journal · Planning

A luxury Christmas and New Year in Egypt

Securing the best boats and suites — what the festive weeks are really like, where to spend 25 and 31 December, and what sells out first.

Islam Hussein  ·  September 2026  ·  16 minute read

By Islam Hussein, Egyptologist guide · crowd notes checked by Soliman Ahmed, Egyptologist guide · Last updated September 2026

Christmas in Egypt: the short answer

Quick answer. Christmas and New Year are Egypt's busiest and most expensive weeks, running from about 20 December to the first days of January. Days in Luxor and Aswan are warm and dry, mornings are cold, and the major sites are crowded by mid-morning. The best dahabiyas and river-view suites sell out first, so secure the boat before anything else. With private, well-timed days it remains one of the finest times to travel — and our festive journey, Christmas & New Year on the Nile, puts Christmas on your own chartered dahabiya and New Year above the First Cataract.

WhereThe Nile Valley (Luxor, Aswan and the river between), Cairo and Giza, the Red Sea
Peak datesAbout 20 December to 4 January. Coptic Christmas falls on 7 January
WeatherLuxor and Aswan: days about 23–25 °C, nights about 6–10 °C. Cairo: about 20 °C by day. Desert nights near freezing (typical averages)
Best hour of the dayOpening time at the major sites; late afternoon at Karnak and Kom Ombo
Time needed10–14 nights for Cairo plus the Nile at a festive pace
When to bookAs early as you can. We accept festive bookings up to 30 days before departure, subject to availability; the dahabiya is always the first thing to secure
Extra costs to expectPeak hotel rates, and compulsory gala dinners at some hotels on 24 and 31 December. On our festive journey, the New Year's Eve dinner is included
Worth the extra ticketSeti I (KV17) in the Valley of the Kings, EGP 2,000, included on our festive journey
Private accessPermits such as The Empty Plateau, requested date by date and confirmed before you book
Good forFamilies tied to school holidays, couples, multi-generational groups on a chartered boat
With SillageChristmas & New Year on the Nile, 14 days with six nights on a chartered dahabiya, €9,999 per person for up to 12 travellers (as of September 2026)

Most people who ask us about a luxury Christmas in Egypt are asking two questions at once. Is it worth going in the busiest weeks of the year? And is it already too late? The honest answers are "usually, yes" and "not yet, but soon".

This guide covers what the festive weeks are really like, where to spend 25 and 31 December, how Coptic Christmas on 7 January differs, and what sells out first. It is written by the team at Sillage Égypte, the private Egypt journey designer. Our Egyptologists have stood at these monuments through many festive seasons — usually at the hours the crowds haven't reached yet.

Reading this in October?

You can still travel this December. You'll be choosing from what remains rather than from everything, so the order of decisions matters more than usual:

  1. Ask about the boat first. A chartered dahabiya is the scarcest piece of the season. If one is free for your dates, everything else can be built around it.
  2. Be flexible by a day or two. Starting after 26 December, or ending before 31 December, often opens up boats and suites that are taken across the peak nights.
  3. Put Aswan before Luxor. Aswan's historic hotels fill early, but Aswan as a whole is quieter than Luxor over the festive days.
  4. Have an overland plan B. If no dahabiya is free, a private car along the river, sleeping in a different hotel at each stage, still gives you the quiet hours at the temples.
  5. Book by late November. We accept festive bookings up to 30 days before departure, subject to availability, but choice narrows every week.

Send us your dates through the planning page and a journey designer will tell you, within 24 hours, what is genuinely still possible.

What is Christmas and New Year in Egypt actually like?

Warm, bright days, cold nights, peak crowds, and a festive mood found mostly in hotels, on boats and in Coptic churches. Egypt is a Muslim-majority country, so 25 December is an ordinary working day; Coptic Christmas on 7 January is the national public holiday.

Weather in late December

Late December in Upper Egypt is dry and sunny, with days around 23–25 °C in Luxor and Aswan and nights that drop to about 6–10 °C. Cairo is cooler, near 20 °C by day. In the Western Desert, nights camping in the White Desert or at Siwa can approach freezing.

The practical consequence is layers. A 6 am start in the Valley of the Kings or on a dahabiya deck is genuinely cold; by noon you'll want a hat. Rain is almost unknown south of Cairo, though Alexandria gets winter showers.

Crowds: when the peak is, and where it bites

The festive peak runs from around 20 December to 4 January, when European and North American school holidays overlap. It is felt most at the Valley of the Kings, Karnak, the Giza plateau, Philae and Abu Simbel.

The reason is what we call the convoy — not the old police escorts on the desert roads, but our shorthand for mass tourism: the large cruise ships and coach groups that reach the same site at the same hour. At Christmas there are simply more of them. Between about 9 am and 1 pm, the famous tombs and halls are at their fullest.

How Egypt marks 25 December

25 December isn't a public holiday in Egypt, and sites, shops and museums keep normal hours. Hotels and dahabiyas mark it with decorations and a Christmas Eve or Christmas Day dinner. In Cairo, several Western churches hold services on 25 December, among them All Saints' Cathedral in Zamalek (Anglican).

New Year's Eve in Egypt

On 31 December, most large hotels in Cairo, Luxor, Aswan and the Red Sea resorts host a gala dinner, and some make it compulsory for guests staying that night, with a supplement priced per person. On our festive journey, Christmas & New Year on the Nile, the New Year's Eve dinner is included, whichever hotel you're in on the night.

On a dahabiya, New Year's Eve is usually a dinner on deck at a quiet mooring. Cairo has the fireworks and the parties. If you'd rather see in the year quietly, choose the setting first and the hotel second.

Where to spend Christmas and New Year in Egypt

For most couples and families, the best place to be over Christmas or New Year is the Nile south of Luxor — on a dahabiya or in Aswan — with Cairo before or after. Families who want rest after the monuments do well to end by the Red Sea.

WhereWhat the festive days feel likeBest forHonest downside
On a dahabiya, Esna to AswanQuiet riverbank moorings, dinner on deck, very few other peopleCouples; families or friends who charter the whole boatThe scarcest thing to book; evenings on deck are cold
AswanSlower, softer: terraces above the First Cataract, Nubian villages, PhilaeCouples, older travellers, second-time visitorsThe historic hotels book first; gala dinners at some

The Red Sea (Hurghada, Sharm el-Sheikh)Sun, water warm enough for most swimmers, days of doing nothingFamilies finishing a Nile journeyNot a cultural setting; resorts at full festive rates
The Western Desert (Siwa, White Desert)Silence, stars, almost no one elseReturning visitorsNights near freezing if you camp

A shape that works well for many travellers is Christmas on the river and New Year in Aswan or Cairo. For Aswan, see our Aswan guide and afternoon tea above the Nile.

Dahabiya, cruise ship or overland over the festive weeks?

A dahabiya is the calmest way to spend Christmas or New Year on the Nile, but also the hardest to book. A large cruise ship is easier to find but puts you inside the convoy. Travelling overland by private car is the most flexible, sleeping in a different hotel at each stage. A dahabiya is a traditional shallow-draught Nile sailing boat with a handful of cabins and a full crew.

DahabiyaLarge cruise shipOverland by private car
GuestsAbout eight cabins on the boats we charterOften 100 or moreOnly your party
Where you sleepRiverbank moorings away from townsTown quays, often several ships abreastA hotel at each stage
Festive dinnerSmall, on deck or in the saloonA ballroom-style galaThe hotel's gala, if it has one
Timing at sitesArranged around the quiet hoursUsually the same schedule as other shipsYou set the hour
How early to bookEarliest of allLaterDepends on the hotels chosen
Best forCouples, families chartering, slower travellersTravellers on a fixed ship scheduleThose who want a suite every night or have fewer days

Why dahabiyas sell out first at Christmas

There are relatively few dahabiyas on the Nile, each with only a handful of cabins, and each boat makes only one or two sailings across the festive dates. Whole-boat charters for Christmas week are especially scarce. We charter the whole boat for the festive journey: about eight cabins, for your party of up to 12 travellers and nobody else.

Our festive journey: Christmas & New Year on the Nile

Christmas & New Year on the Nile is built around everything in this guide: the boat secured first, the monuments at their quiet hours, and 25 and 31 December kept light. Fourteen days, 21 December to 3 January, at €9,999 per person for up to 12 travellers (as of September 2026).

  • 21–22 December, Cairo. The Egyptian Museum at opening, Coptic Cairo already dressed for Christmas, Khan el-Khalili at dusk.
  • 23 December, Luxor. Karnak from 3 pm into sunset, Luxor Temple lit after dark.
  • 24 December, Christmas Eve. The Valley of the Kings at 6 am with Seti I included, then aboard your chartered dahabiya at Esna for Christmas Eve dinner.
  • 25–29 December, the river. Christmas Day under sail with nothing planned, then El-Kab, Edfu after the ships leave, Gebel el-Silsila and Kom Ombo at dusk.
  • 30–31 December, the deep south. Philae on an early boat, a night beside the temples of Abu Simbel, and New Year's Eve dinner, included, above the First Cataract in Aswan.
  • 1–3 January, Giza. A slow New Year's Day, then the Pyramids at opening and the Grand Egyptian Museum, with two nights at Mena House.

If you'd rather start from a signature journey, The Complete Egypt and The Nile & the Red Sea can both be arranged over the festive weeks. Their published prices (from €7,500 and €7,999 per person) are for standard dates; festive dates carry a peak-season supplement, shown in your proposal.

Coptic Christmas on 7 January: what it is, and can visitors attend?

Coptic Christmas is celebrated on 7 January by the Coptic Orthodox Church, Egypt's largest Christian community, and it is a national public holiday. Visitors can often attend the Christmas Eve liturgy on the night of 6 January, provided they dress modestly and accept security checks.

Why Coptic Christmas falls on 7 January

The Coptic Church keeps Christmas on 29 Kiahk in the Coptic calendar, which currently corresponds to 7 January in the Gregorian calendar. It is preceded by the Nativity Fast, 43 days during which many Copts eat no meat or dairy. The Christmas Eve meal breaks the fast.

The Christmas Eve liturgy on 6 January

Pope Tawadros II usually leads the Christmas Eve liturgy at the Cathedral of the Nativity of Christ in the New Administrative Capital, east of Cairo. Parish churches across Cairo, including St Mark's Coptic Orthodox Cathedral in Abbassia, hold their own services, often late into the night. Attendance isn't guaranteed; your guide can ask a parish on your behalf.

Etiquette for visitors

  • Cover shoulders and knees, and bring a light layer; churches are cold at night.
  • Expect security screening at the door, and carry your passport.
  • Ask before photographing, and never use flash during the liturgy.
  • Arrive early, and plan to stay; leaving mid-service is noticed.

A quieter way to mark it: Coptic Cairo

In the days around 7 January, Coptic Cairo is festive but calm. The Hanging Church and the Church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus (Abu Serga) make an easy half-day.

How early should you book Christmas in Egypt?

As early as you can. We accept festive bookings up to 30 days before departure, subject to availability, but the best dahabiyas and river-view suites are usually taken long before then. If you're reading this in autumn for this December, it isn't hopeless — see Reading this in October? above.

What sells out first

  1. Dahabiya cabins and whole-boat charters for sailings that include 24–25 or 31 December.
  2. River-view and cataract-view suites at the historic hotels in Aswan and Luxor.
  3. Rooms at Abu Simbel, where there are very few hotels.
  4. Domestic flights on the busiest days, around 23 December and 1–3 January.
  5. Private access permits, which are requested date by date.

Festive pricing, minimum stays and gala supplements

Most hotels charge their highest rates of the year between Christmas and New Year, and some elsewhere require a compulsory gala dinner. The hotels on our festive route don't require a minimum stay, and on the festive journey the New Year's Eve dinner is included. Once confirmed, the price is guaranteed, except for increases caused by government action, taxes or significant currency changes, as set out in our booking terms.

Special access over the holidays

Private access — such as The Empty Plateau at Giza or The Empty Museum at the Grand Egyptian Museum — depends on official permission for each date. It is never guaranteed, and over the festive weeks demand is higher. Sillage confirms whether it is possible, and what it costs, before you book.

Secure the boat first. Everything else can be built around it.

How to see the monuments without the festive crowds

The way to see Egypt's monuments quietly in the busiest weeks is to be there at opening or in the last hours of the day, and to sleep where the day-trippers don't. These notes come from our Egyptologists, and Soliman Ahmed has checked each one on festive-season mornings.

  1. The Valley of the Kings at opening. Enter when the gates open at 6 am and you have roughly two hours before the ships' groups arrive. Add Seti I (KV17): its EGP 2,000 extra ticket keeps it quieter than the tombs on the standard ticket, and it is included on our festive journey.
  2. Karnak in the late afternoon. Sunset in Luxor in late December is just after 5 pm. From about 3 pm the groups thin out, and the low sun lights the columns of the Hypostyle Hall from the side.
  3. Abu Simbel overnight. Most visitors arrive from Aswan in the morning and leave by early afternoon. Stay the night and you see the temples in evening light and again at dawn. Both The Grand Tour and our festive journey include a night at Abu Simbel.
  4. Philae on the first boat. The island temple is at its best before 9 am, when the launches from the quay are still few.
  5. Keep 25 and 31 December light. Plan a felucca sail or a slow morning, not a major site; dinners run late on both nights.
  6. Dendera by river. The Temple of Hathor at Dendera draws far fewer people than Karnak and has some of the best-preserved ceiling colour in Egypt. The Temple by River reaches it by a day's sail from Luxor.

Who festive Egypt suits, and who should go in January instead

Christmas and New Year in Egypt suit families bound to school holidays, couples who want a festive table on the river, and multi-generational groups who can charter a dahabiya together. They suit less well anyone who could move their dates.

Mid-to-late January brings much the same weather, noticeably fewer people and far more choice of boats and suites. If your dates are free, we'll say so — it's part of why we'll sometimes talk you out of a trip. For month-by-month detail, see when to go to Egypt.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Leaving the boat until last: book the dahabiya first and build the rest around it.
  • Packing only summer clothes; early mornings and boat decks are cold.
  • Putting the Valley of the Kings or Karnak at 10 am on 27 December.
  • Overlooking compulsory gala dinners when comparing hotel prices.
  • Scheduling a very early flight on 1 January after a late New Year's Eve.
